#2129. English football’s top 25 biggest football clubs named and ranked by AI

A debate that will rage forever but one that remains fierce in English football is who is the biggest club in the land - and, between sets of supporters, whose club is bigger than the others.

The birthplace of the sport, football is perhaps the biggest cultural, political and emotional phenomenon in English society and wanting to be a fan of a club towards the top of its notional hierarchy does mean a lot to many.

Be it based on titles won, trophies gained, the amount of match-going supporters or even fans from overseas; the size of a club is not something decided empirically and therefore the debate will always rage on.

Subjective and controversial no matter how it is discussed or deciphered, there is a new form of trying to find a definitive answer in the modern world and that is with the use of AI - and so we have asked ChatGPT to rank the 25 biggest clubs in English football - whatever that really does mean.

Whether it be years spent in the top-flight, the size of a club’s fan base, their trophies won or historical significance; here is the list of the top 25 biggest clubs according on AI.

Squeezed into the 25 biggest clubs in England according to ChatGPT are Portsmouth, with their two league titles and historically excellent support the reasons outlined for being in the top 25.

Pompey, known for a raucous atmosphere at Fratton Park, entered into the Football League in 1920 and won successive titles shortly after the Second World War. The now Championship outfit fell out of the top four in 1959 and only experienced one further season before a seven-year stint on the Premier League during the 2000s - a period that saw them win the FA Cup, as well as reach another final, and play European football, too.

One of the oldest teams in the Football League or the EFL or, simply, English football and football altogether; next on AI’s list of the top 25 biggest clubs is Stoke City.

Established in 1863, Stoke have one major honour to their name with the 1972 League Cup, having been FA Cup runners-up to Manchester City in 2011. The Potters have spent large swathes of their history in the top-flight with their most recent stint lasting ten seasons between 2008 and 2018 before a frustrating malaise back down in the Championship, albeit challenging again this time around.

The first ever Football League champions marks Preston North End out as 23rd on AI’s list with the history and tradition of English football perhaps most well represented by Preston’s early dominance.

North End won the league and FA Cup double in the 1888-89 season as the original ‘invicibles’ without losing across the campaign before backing up their league title a season later. That history has had to count for a lot for PNE, though, having not been a top-flight club since the days of Sir Tom Finney; relegated in 1960-61 and yet to return as they now battle against relegation down to League One this season.

From the city of the oldest football club in the world, Sheffield FC, 22nd on ChatGPT’s list of the biggest club in England are four-time FA Cup winners Sheffield United.

The Blades, who also have a league title to their name winning the league in the 1897-98 campaign, are one of the more storied cup teams and one of the more historic, albeit not a founding member. They achieved promotion to the top-flight in 1894 and have remained there until 1934 before yo-yoing between the top two divisions until the 1980s. That yo-yoing has returned in the last decade or so with their last seven full seasons being split three in the top-flight and four in the second-tier.

Next up on the list chosen or suggested by AI is another Championship outfit and this time it is two-time English champion Burnley, who are struggling down at the bottom end of the second-tier now.

A founding member of the Football League, Burnley have spent much of the last decade and a bit in the Premier League, having not been in the top-flight from 1975-76 until one season in the 2009-10 campaign. The Clarets, who won the league in both 1921 and 1960, as well as an FA Cup in 1913, are one of few teams to have won the English title while also spending a fair bit of time in the fourth-tier.

Having touched upon several clubs with historic significance, next on the list is one of the modern day ‘bigger clubs’ with AI putting Leicester City 20th on the list.

Famously, The Foxes produced a ‘great escape’ before winning the 2015-16 Premier League title - becoming the first outsider of 5000/1 odds to ever win in any sport. The next half a decade saw them begin to cement themselves as top four challengers as well as then win the FA Cup but the last few years has not gone well and they now reside back in League One - and struggling to find the consistency to bounce back after back-to-back relegations.

A local rival of Leicester in the East Midlands and another team struggling this season is next on the list with two-time English champions and Football League founding member Derby County.

Raucous crowds at Pride Park have dampened this season with The Rams struggling down at the bottom end of the Championship table. Two-time league winners in the 1970s, Derby regularly knocked on the door of promotion during the 2010s but they have spent just one season in the Premier League, setting the record for the lowest points tally of 11, since the 2001-02 campaign.

Rated as the bigger of the Sheffield clubs by AI; next on the list at number 18 are United’s arch-rivals Sheffield Wednesday with their four league titles, three FA Cups and one League Cup.

The Owls are again one of the more storied teams in English football with dominance at both the start of the 1900s and in the late-1920s. Wednesday could perhaps be argued to be the biggest sleeping giant in English given football, given that they haven’t been in the top-flight since relegation in the 1999-00 campaign, having previously spent most of their history at that level. They are one of two clubs outside of the top two divisions to be in ChatGPT's list.

Perhaps surprisingly low down on the list considering their well acknowledged European Cup history; Nottingham Forest are rated the 17th biggest club in England according to AI.

ChatGPT suggests Nottingham Forest’s two triumphs in the European Cup are only enough for 17th. During the era of Brian Clough at the City Ground, Forest won a league title, four League Cups, the Community Shield, two European Cups and the Super Cup. Outside of that 18-year reign, though, Forest’s other major honours both came in the FA Cup in 1898 and 1959. Now back in the Premier League; it is where many believe the club should reside.

Next up on ChatGPT’s list of the 25 biggest clubs in England is a storied stalwart of the top two divisions in English football from the midlands, West Bromwich Albion.

Five-time FA Cup winners and founding members of the Football League, West Brom also have a league title under their belt, won in 1920. Albion have had some real highs as a part of English football’s furniture with their late 70s team of Laurie Cunningham, Brendan Baston, Cyrille Regis, Tony Brown, John Wile and Bryan Robson one that is fondly remembered by many a neutral. On only one occasion ever in their 148-year history have The Baggies not been playing in either the top-flight or the second-tier.

#2128. Chelsea World Cup Knockout Load Gives Xabi Alonso Pre-Season Problem

Chelsea’s World Cup contingent has moved from a group-stage watchlist into a genuine Xabi Alonso planning problem.

Chelsea’s own tournament update confirms that Enzo Fernandez, Mike Penders, Moises Caicedo, Kendry Paez, Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato have reached the Round of 32.

England have also progressed after their final Group L win over Panama, which keeps Reece James and Trevoh Chalobah inside the wider knockout picture.

For supporters, that is a status marker. For Alonso, it is where summer pride starts to become pre-season compression.

The concern is not simply volume. It is where the minutes are landing.

Enzo has not missed a minute for Argentina, while Caicedo has remained central for Ecuador and captained them in the 2-1 win over Germany.

Those are not fringe workloads. They are the two midfield profiles Chelsea have built large parts of their control game around.

Alonso’s first Chelsea pre-season was always going to demand clarity through the middle of the pitch.

Instead, the players most central to that reset are still operating in knockout football.

Caicedo’s Ecuador role is the cleanest example. Read Chelsea has already assessed how his captaincy display against Germany strengthened his leadership case, but the next layer is more complicated.

Every additional knockout tie gives him more tournament rhythm, more authority and more fatigue.

Argentina’s route against Cape Verde keeps him on a glamorous stage at exactly the moment Chelsea need to settle his role, mood and tactical responsibilities under Alonso.

If Madrid-related noise continues around him, the club cannot afford a sluggish July handover.

Reece James started England’s first two matches before a hamstring issue ruled him out of the Panama game, according to the Guardian.

England still topped the group and moved into a last-32 tie with DR Congo, but James’ situation is exactly the kind of detail Chelsea’s medical team will monitor closely.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader issue was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

Enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

That is a spine issue, not a fringe issue.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Those details do not bed in properly when key players arrive in drips after a major summer tournament.

Players returning from knockout football can bring competitive sharpness that closed-door friendlies cannot replicate.

Caicedo captaining Ecuador through pressure games matters. Enzo playing high-leverage minutes for Argentina matters.

Gusto and Hato absorbing tournament detail also helps Chelsea’s defensive reset.

But Chelsea cannot treat every tournament minute as clean preparation.

Alonso must decide who returns straight into tactical work, who needs a genuine pause and who can handle August without creating an avoidable injury bill by September.

That is where the James situation feels central.

If Chelsea’s captain carries a World Cup hamstring warning, the club’s right-sided structure becomes more than a selection debate.

It becomes an availability question that touches Gusto, the wider defensive rebuild and the need for control from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

This is the hidden cost of a strong international footprint.

Chelsea want players good enough to survive deep into tournaments.

Alonso now has to make sure that status does not leave his first league weeks short of the very control those players are meant to provide.

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal moved up to third in the Champions League table after beating Slavia Prague 2-1 at the Fortuna Arena.

Noni Madueke opened the scoring after nine minutes, finishing calmly after Viktor Gyokeres sent him through on goal.

The Swedish striker then doubled Arsenal’s advantage with an excellent finish in the 38th minute. However, a much stronger second-half performance from Slavia made for an uncomfortable finish.

Wiktor Nowak scored a late goal to put pressure on the Gunners. They held on to take all three points.

Mikel Arteta made six changes from the Liverpool win on Sunday. William Saliba returns to the squad after his back injury.

The defender was left on the bench, with Ezri Konsa playing alongside Gabriel Magalhães in central defence.

Arsenal started brightly and took control of the game when they won the long ball forward. Gyokeres beat his man and found Madueke with a clever through ball.

The winger used his pace to get into the penalty area before sliding his finish through goalkeeper Nazar Domchak’s legs.

Arsenal continued to create chances, with Mikel Merino going close on several occasions. Domchak also produced an important save to deny the midfielder from close range.

Merino eventually helped Arsenal extend their lead. After winning possession in the Slavia half, Declan Rice found Gyokeres, who exchanged passes with the Spaniard before curling a superb finish into the far corner.

The visitors could have added a third before the break. Gabriel’s header from a corner was cleared off the line.

Arsenal appeared to be in control at half-time.

But Slavia upped the tempo and started to create more space, forcing Arsenal into a defensive stance. Early on, Oskar Kubiak fired a long-range shot, forcing David Raya to push it away.

Arteta got increasingly frustrated as Arsenal struggled to hold on to the ball and dominate the midfield.

They tried to keep pressing, but Arsenal struggled to create much at the other end. Madueke did get into a good position to shoot from an angle but didn’t have enough power to cause any problems for Domchak.

Slavia were denied a goal when Gabriel headed the ball away from the goal line. Raya made a brilliant stop to keep the shot out while the penalty area was crowded.

The Arsenal keeper made another stunning save as Kubiak powered a header from a cross. Raya deflected the ball onto the post to keep his team ahead by two goals.

Slavia scored their breakthrough goal in the 90th minute after David Jurasek played a low cross from the left. Nowak was able to run into the box to score past Raya.

It created a nervy few minutes of added time as Arsenal had to defend their lead.

Slavia could find no way back into the game as Stepan Chaloupek headed wide and Mikulas Konecny threatened in the dying moments, but his effort lacked confidence as Raya made light work of saving.

Arsenal secured their third win in their last four Champions League games to move to 10 points and into third place in the group stage.

The Gunners have now gone unbeaten in their last ten Champions League away games to set a new club record.

However, Arteta will be looking for a much better display from his side when they resume action in the Premier League against Hull City on Saturday.

#2126. Manchester United defence: Why Carrick must trust Yoro and Heaven

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United endured another embarrassing draw against 10-man Tottenham after failing to register their second win despite bringing in a plethora of players.

Manchester United invested heavily last season in their attacking options, bringing in Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha.

This season, they overhauled their midfield. United spent massively on Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos. Despite spending massively, they have failed to produce the control they would have expected in the midfield. The lack of control was evident in the recent Tottenham game, where Mainoo-Tielemans partnership failed to control the game collectively.

The midfield question was covered in our recent report as well, highlighting a lack of control and carried comments from Gary Neville and Jamie Redknapp.

The bigger question is when United will strengthen their defence. As per our previous report as well, Manchester United are planning to overhaul their defence in the upcoming transfer windows.

United were heavily linked with several left backs but eventually failed to bring any one. The situation left Luke Shaw as the only senior option in the position, while Patrick Dorgu is used upfront by Michael Carrick.

Harry Amass is another option for Michael Carrick, but he is only here because of a failed transfer move. He has been rarely used at left back as Dalot and Mazraoui get the nod in the position ahead of him.

The situation at right-back isn’t all good either. Diogo Dalot is the first option there, but he rarely provides the assurance that puts Michael Carrick at ease. Noussair Mazraoui is the second choice at right-back, but his attacking numbers aren’t great either.

Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez form up United’s centre-back pairing while Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven are used all over the defensive line in rotation when needed. Yoro was used at right-back against Tottenham while Heaven arrived as left-back towards the end of the game.

Manchester United’s season hasn’t been defensively strong or anywhere near being good. They have conceded goals in all Premier League games and only kept one clean sheet against Sabah in the Champions League.

Lisandro Martinez has come under scrutiny after errors on four occasions. Against Ipswich Town, Manchester United won 5-2, but his error resulted in Ipswich’s second goal.

His own goal against Fulham gave away two points at Craven Cottage in the 1-1 draw. Another error led to Solanke’s goal against Tottenham, when he took his eyes off the ball.

His injury concerns are another aspect, and maybe Michael Carrick needs to make a decision.

Manchester United’s success depended heavily on youth over the years. When pundits questioned them, Sir Alex Ferguson gave them the chance to prove them wrong. Alan Hansen made the famous quote “You can’t win anything with kids” on the BBC’s Match of the Day on August 19, 1995. United did exactly that, played youth and went on to win everything.

Michael Carrick needs to do exactly that. He needs to trust youth and allow them to make mistakes. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven arrived as massive potentials, but they haven’t been given the license to express themselves, without fearing for their places. Both the youngsters have rarely started together or in a stretch of games. It is maybe time for them to take their chances.

Michael Carrick needs to keep Harry Maguire as a senior experienced figure around them. There is no doubt over Martinez’s ability, but he is not the answer to United’s long-term problem. United need to blend youth with experience as their identity moving forward. Lisandro Martinez perhaps isn’t the answer to United’s problem.

A defensive revival expected in the upcoming transfer windows needs to happen now. It must happen with chances to the Youth. Michael Carrick needs to be brave enough and throw the youngsters in the mix. What it will bring is a long-term solution. They need to experience the errors and pressures that will shape them in football.
